hints: Start by picturing the direction of the message - where does it first arrive at the neurone and where must it finally leave?
Think about the receiving end - what short branching structures feed into the part that contains the nucleus?
Recall what a very active cell needs a lot of - which organelles would you expect in the cell body to make proteins and release energy?
Now follow the long fibre that carries the impulse away - is there one or many, and what is found at its far tip?
Remember this is a motor neurone in a vertebrate - what fatty wrapping surrounds much of that long fibre?
If that wrapping is not continuous, what are the gaps called and why are they important to mention for full marks?
walkthrough:
Picture the Receiving End**
You can think of a motor neurone as having a clear one-way layout. Short, highly branched dendrites collect incoming signals and funnel them toward the cell body. The cell body, also called the soma, is at one end of the cell and contains the nucleus.

Zoom Into the Cell Body**
The cell body is the metabolic centre. It is packed with many mitochondria to supply ATP for active processes like maintaining ion gradients, and a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum, seen as Nissl's granules, to make the proteins and neurotransmitter-related enzymes and channel proteins the neurone needs.

Follow the Long Transmitting Fibre**
Leading away from the cell body is a single long axon. That length is what lets a motor neurone carry impulses from the spinal cord all the way to a muscle. At the far end, furthest from the cell body, the axon branches to end in swollen synaptic knobs or boutons that will pass the message on.

Add the Insulation**
Much of the axon is wrapped by Schwann cells that form the fatty myelin sheath. The sheath is not continuous - it is interrupted at regular gaps called nodes of Ranvier where the axon membrane is exposed. Including dendrites, cell body contents, single axon, synaptic knobs, myelin and nodes gives you the full structural description.

Final answer: Motor neurone has short branched dendrites leading to a cell body / soma containing the nucleus; cell body contains many mitochondria and much RER / Nissl's granules; a single long axon extends from cell body; synaptic knobs / boutons at end furthest from cell body; axon surrounded by Schwann cells forming myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier.

hints: Start with the resting state - inside negative relative to outside - then ask what must change in membrane permeability to reverse that.
Focus on the first ion to move - which positive ion is more concentrated outside and rushes in when its channels open?
Link that movement to voltage - what happens to the potential difference when positive charge enters, up to about +40 mV?
An action potential is brief, so what must quickly happen to those first channels, and which second type of channel then opens?
Think opposite movement for the second ion - which ion leaves the axon to make the inside negative again?
Now shift from one patch of membrane to the next - how does charge spread sideways to trigger the next region?
Recall the role of the fatty layer - how does myelin affect ion movement across the axon membrane?
If ions can only cross at gaps, where exactly can a new action potential be regenerated?
Put it together to explain speed and direction - what name is given to jumping from gap to gap and why is transmission one-way?
walkthrough:
Depolarisation - Sodium Rushes In**
At rest the inside is negative. When stimulated, voltage-gated $Na^{+}$ channels open in the membrane. Because $Na^{+}$ is more concentrated outside, $Na^{+}$ diffuses rapidly into the axon. That influx of positive charge makes the inside less negative, then positive, reaching about +40 mV. That reversal is depolarisation.

Repolarisation - Sodium Stops, Potassium Leaves**
Almost immediately the $Na^{+}$ channels close. Now voltage-gated $K^{+}$ channels open. $K^{+}$ is more concentrated inside, so $K^{+}$ moves out of the cell down its concentration gradient. Loss of positive charge makes the inside negative again. That restoration is repolarisation. A brief hyperpolarisation and refractory period may follow.

How the Wave Moves On - Local Circuits**
The influx of $Na^{+}$ at one point creates local circuits - positive charge spreads sideways inside the axon and attracts ions outside. This depolarises the adjacent region of membrane to threshold, so its $Na^{+}$ channels open and a new action potential forms there. In this way the action potential is regenerated along the axon.

Why Myelin Makes It Fast - Saltatory Conduction**
In a myelinated neurone the Schwann cells and fatty myelin sheath act as electrical insulation. They prevent ion movement and depolarisation across the myelinated regions. Ions can only cross at the exposed nodes of Ranvier where there are many voltage-gated channels.

Jumping From Node to Node**
So the action potential / depolarisation occurs only at the nodes. Local circuits spread charge rapidly under the insulated myelin to the next node, where a full action potential is regenerated. It appears to jump from node to node. This is saltatory conduction, which is much faster and saves energy. Because the previous region is in its refractory period, transmission is unidirectional.

Final answer: Voltage-gated $Na^{+}$ channels open, $Na^{+}$ enters axon causing depolarisation to about +40 mV; then $Na^{+}$ channels close and voltage-gated $K^{+}$ channels open, $K^{+}$ moves out causing repolarisation; local circuits spread depolarisation; myelin sheath insulates and prevents ion movement so action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier, giving saltatory conduction from node to node and unidirectional transmission.
